name: Hip Flexion Isolation
definition: A narrow unilateral open-chain bodyweight task in which a straight working leg rises from a supine, table-supported start to the athlete's active hip-flexion end range and then returns under control. The reviewed protocol directly measured psoas major, rectus femoris, rectus abdominis, external oblique, and the combined internal-oblique/transversus-abdominis site across the concentric, end-range, and eccentric phases. Iliopsoas is primary and rectus femoris secondary; the visible iliopsoas region necessarily combines the directly measured psoas major with an unseparated iliacus mesh. Abs and obliques receive conservative trunk-and-pelvis stability credit. The study does not establish one numeric hip endpoint, a standardized cadence or hold duration, or a zero-motion pelvis or spine, so those details are not invented. Tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, and the adductors receive no role merely from general hip-flexor capability. Loaded raises, standing marches, hanging or captain-chair raises, knee raises, sit-ups, V-ups, machine or cable flexion, and any movement that deliberately adds spinal, pelvic, or knee motion remain outside this contract.

execution.startingPosition: Lie on your back with your torso and pelvis supported on a table and both legs straight.
execution.movement: Raise the working leg as far as you can while keeping the knee straight.
execution.endpoint: End the raise at the highest point you can reach with a straight knee.
execution.controlledJoints: Keep the other leg supported and the working knee straight. Keep the effort centered on the working hip without deliberately adding spinal, pelvic, or knee motion.
execution.supportAndPosture: Let the table support your torso, pelvis, and resting leg.
disqualifyingCompensations: Bending the working knee turns the straight-leg raise into a knee raise.
Rolling the pelvis backward to lift higher turns the hip raise into a sit-up.
execution.sideOrDirection: Finish the set with one leg, then repeat with the other leg.
